Juniper
JOO-nih-per
noun
From the Latin juniperus. In the AV it renders the Hebrew rothem, the white broom of the desert — a tall, scanty shrub of the southern wilderness whose thin shade is the only shelter for miles and whose roots make the hottest and longest-burning coals.

Biblical Definition

The juniper of Scripture is the desert broom, and it is chiefly known by one man who slept under it. Elijah, fresh from Carmel and fleeing Jezebel’s oath, went a day’s journey into the wilderness, sat down under a juniper tree, and asked to die (1Ki 19:4). Here is a true prophet of the LORD, of like passions with us (Jas 5:17), sunk so low that death looks like mercy. Mark how the LORD deals with him. There is no rebuke first, and no indulgence either. There is sleep: “And as he lay and slept under a juniper tree, behold, then an angel touched him, and said unto him, Arise and eat” (1Ki 19:5). There is food: “a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head” (1Ki 19:6). There is a second touch and a reason — “the journey is too great for thee” (1Ki 19:7). Then, and only then, forty days to Horeb, the wind and earthquake and fire, the still small voice, a searching question twice asked, a fresh commission, and the word that seven thousand knees had never bowed to Baal. God restored His prophet by bread and sleep and then by His word, and He sent him back to work. The wood serves elsewhere as an emblem of judgment — the false tongue is answered with “sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper” (Psa 120:4) — and its roots are the meat of the destitute (Job 30:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

The desert broom of the AV; a scanty shrub giving thin shade, whose roots yield the fiercest coals.

JUNIPER, a shrub or low tree of the waste places; in Scripture the desert broom, Hebrew rothem.

From the Latin juniperus.

Its shade is thin, yet it is the only shelter in the southern wilderness.

Its roots burn hot and long, whence “coals of juniper” (Psa 120:4).

Elijah sat and slept beneath it when he requested to die (1Ki 19:4–5).

Key Scripture

1Ki 19:5 — "And as he lay and slept under a juniper tree, behold, then an angel touched him, and said unto him, Arise and eat."

1Ki 19:6 — "And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again."

1Ki 19:7 — "And the angel of the LORD came again the second time, and touched him, and said, Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee."

Psa 120:4 — "Sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper."

Modern Corruption

The juniper text is now commonly preached as a case study, with the diagnosis kept and the LORD’s word at Horeb cut out.

expand to see more

The live corruption is the therapeutic reduction of 1 Kings 19. The chapter is handed over to the counselling clinic: Elijah is a study in exhaustion, the angel’s cake becomes a lesson in nutrition, the sleep becomes a lesson in rest, and the sermon ends there — before Horeb, before the still small voice, before the twice-repeated question that searched the prophet’s heart, before the commission that sent him back to anoint kings, and before the seven thousand that answered his self-pity with fact. What is left is a chapter about a tired man managing himself, when Scripture wrote a chapter about the living God restoring His servant. Bread and sleep are genuinely there, and God gave them; but He gave them as the first mercies of a longer dealing, not as the whole cure. Strip out the word of the LORD and the passage no longer preaches the LORD at all.

The opposite error must be named too: the affected piety that denies a saint can sink. Some pulpits treat Elijah’s request to die as simple unbelief to be scolded, and so they teach the afflicted brother to hide. Scripture is more honest and more tender than either party. It records the prophet’s words without excusing them and without shaming him for them; it names his despondency, and it shows God answering with an angel’s touch rather than a lecture. The Psalms speak the same way — “Why art thou cast down, O my soul?… hope thou in God” (Psa 42:11) — a real question honestly asked, and then the soul commanded back to its Rock. The pattern is: the LORD supplies the body, speaks to the soul, and restores the man to his work. Neither the clinic nor the scold can do that.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word names the desert broom — thin shade above, fierce coals below.

expand to see more

Juniper — Latin juniperus; in the AV the Hebrew rothem, the desert broom.

It is a scanty shrub of the southern wilderness, its shade the only shelter for miles.

Elijah sat and slept under it and requested that he might die (1Ki 19:4–5).

Its roots yield coals of unusual heat and endurance (Psa 120:4).

Those roots were meat for the destitute in Job’s lament (Job 30:4).

Usage

"Under the juniper tree a true prophet asked to die — and God sent bread, not a rebuke."

"The juniper gives thin shade; the angel’s cake and the cruse of water gave more."

"Coals of juniper burn longest: so the Psalmist pictures the answer to a false tongue."
